sourcedFrom: ELIMIN8R .45 OWNERS manual — REVISED 5.21 (UNKNOWN — not printed in the document)
cleanIntro: Lone Wolf's book for the ELIMIN8R .45 asks for two levels of care. After every shooting session the piston mechanism — piston, spring and piston endcap — comes out, is scrubbed and is greased, and the mount area and baffle threads are kept free of carbon. For a full clean, each of the eight baffles is separated, inspected, cleaned and lubricated, with its O-ring checked. The body and baffles are anodized aluminum, so every chemical used must be safe on it.

steps.title: Host unloaded, magazine out, chamber checked
steps.action: Before you put a hand on the suppressor, make sure the host firearm is unloaded and safe: remove the magazine, then look into and feel the chamber and action to confirm they are empty.
steps.prose: The can sits directly in front of the muzzle, so every minute you spend turning it is a minute your hand is in front of the bore. Lone Wolf asks for both a visual and a manual check, because a glance alone misses a round you cannot see.
steps.quote: Remove the magazine from the firearm. Visually and manually check and clear the chamber and action.
steps.cite: ELIMIN8R .45 OWNERS manual — REVISED 5.21 — 5. INSTALLATION, printed p.9

steps.title: Let it cool to room temperature
steps.action: Wait until the suppressor is back to ambient temperature before you try to take it off. If you cannot wait, use protective measures — gloves or a heat-proof grip — rather than bare hands.
steps.prose: A pistol can that has just been shot is hot enough to burn, and hot threads also bind, which is when people reach for force they should not use.
steps.quote: Let the suppressor cool to ambient temperature before removal.
steps.cite: ELIMIN8R .45 OWNERS manual — REVISED 5.21 — 6. REMOVAL, printed p.11
steps.warn: Be cautious! The suppressor will have become extremely hot after use and could cause burns or injury.

steps.title: Unthread it the way your barrel's thread runs
steps.action: Unscrew the suppressor from the host barrel. Which way it turns depends on the barrel's thread: clockwise for a metric (left-hand) thread, counterclockwise for a standard thread. Know which one your barrel has before you put force on it.
steps.prose: Turning a can the wrong way only tightens it. If it will not move in the direction you expected, stop and check the thread rather than adding force.
steps.quote: To unthread the suppressor turn it clockwise for a metric thread or counterclockwise for a standard thread.
steps.cite: ELIMIN8R .45 OWNERS manual — REVISED 5.21 — 6. REMOVAL, printed p.11

steps.title: Piston endcap, spring and piston out
steps.action: If the can is set up with the piston for a tilting-barrel handgun, take out the piston endcap, the spring and the piston. Lone Wolf names these three pieces as what comes out of the body before a fixed or three-lug mount goes in, and the same three pieces are what the book asks you to clean after every session.
steps.prose: Keep the spring with the piston and endcap so nothing gets lost. If your can wears a fixed barrel spacer, direct-thread mount or three-lug adapter instead, there is no piston to remove.
steps.quote: If you choose to use a fixed mount or three lug mount, remove the piston, spring and piston endcap and install the fixed mount or three lug mount into the suppressor body.
steps.cite: ELIMIN8R .45 OWNERS manual — REVISED 5.21 — 5. INSTALLATION, printed p.10

steps.title: Field strip complete — off the host, piston out
steps.action: With the suppressor off the gun and the piston mechanism out, you have what the routine clean needs. The least maintenance Lone Wolf asks for is keeping the mount area and the baffle threads free of carbon and debris. Separating the baffles is the deep clean.
steps.prose: Carbon left in the mount area is what stops the piston or mount from seating cleanly, and the baffle threads are what hold the whole stack together.
steps.quote: Generally, the minimum maintenance needed is keeping the mount area free of carbon and other debris and the threads of the baffles.
steps.cite: ELIMIN8R .45 OWNERS manual — REVISED 5.21 — 7. CLEANING & MAINTENANCE, printed p.12

steps.title: Scrub the piston parts with a stiff brush and solvent
steps.action: The piston components are steel. Scrub them clean with a stiff brush and a cleaning solvent such as CLP. Lone Wolf asks for this cleaning and lubrication after every shooting session.
steps.prose: Pistol cans foul quickly at the rear, and the piston is the moving part a booster depends on — if it sticks, the host's action can stop cycling.
steps.quote: The piston components are made of steel and can be scrubbed clean using a stiff brush and cleaning solvent, such as Cleaner, Lubricant, Protectant (CLP).
steps.cite: ELIMIN8R .45 OWNERS manual — REVISED 5.21 — 7. CLEANING & MAINTENANCE, printed p.12

steps.title: Clear the carbon out of the piston grooves
steps.action: Work the grooves on the piston until the carbon is out of them. Then give the piston body a light coat of lithium grease.
steps.prose: Carbon packed into the grooves is what makes the piston drag going back into the body. Lone Wolf ties the clean grooves directly to smooth assembly.
steps.quote: To ensure smooth assembly, the grooves on the piston should be thoroughly cleaned, and have carbon removed.
steps.cite: ELIMIN8R .45 OWNERS manual — REVISED 5.21 — 7. CLEANING & MAINTENANCE, printed p.12

steps.title: Only chemicals that are safe on anodized aluminum
steps.action: The body and baffles are aluminum with an anodized finish. Before any solvent goes on them, make sure it is safe for anodized aluminum.
steps.prose: Some aggressive carbon removers attack aluminum and its finish. The steel piston can take a stiff brush and CLP; the body and baffles need more care in what you put on them.
steps.quote: Be aware of what chemicals you choose to use and that they are safe to use with anodized aluminum.
steps.cite: ELIMIN8R .45 OWNERS manual — REVISED 5.21 — 7. CLEANING & MAINTENANCE, printed p.13

deepSteps.title: Separate the baffles
deepSteps.action: With the suppressor off the gun and the piston out, separate each baffle from the stack. The baffles thread together; take them apart one at a time and keep track of how many there are — the can ships with eight.
deepSteps.prose: The book names no tool for this step. The baffles are all identical, so you do not need to note their order.
deepSteps.quote: Each Baffle should be separated, inspected, cleaned, and lubricated.
deepSteps.cite: ELIMIN8R .45 OWNERS manual — REVISED 5.21 — 7. CLEANING & MAINTENANCE, printed p.12

deepSteps.title: Check every baffle O-ring
deepSteps.action: Look at the O-ring on each baffle and check it for damage — cuts, flat spots, or a ring that has stretched out of its groove. Replacement O-rings come from Lone Wolf Arms.
deepSteps.prose: A damaged O-ring is what lets gas and carbon into the threads between baffles, which makes the next take-down harder.
deepSteps.quote: Take note of each O-ring on the baffles and inspect for damage.
deepSteps.cite: ELIMIN8R .45 OWNERS manual — REVISED 5.21 — 7. CLEANING & MAINTENANCE, printed p.12

deepSteps.title: Clean the baffles and their threads
deepSteps.action: Clean each baffle and its threads of carbon and debris, using only chemicals that are safe on anodized aluminum. If you shot the can wet to loosen buildup, dry every part completely afterwards.
deepSteps.prose: The threads matter most: carbon left in them is what makes the stack cross-thread or bind when it goes back together.
deepSteps.quote: After shooting wet, be sure to dry the suppressor components and apply lubricant to the piston mechanism, if being used.
deepSteps.cite: ELIMIN8R .45 OWNERS manual — REVISED 5.21 — 7. CLEANING & MAINTENANCE, printed p.13

cleaning.name: PISTON MECHANISM
tasks: Piston, spring and piston endcap — cleaned and lubricated after every shooting session
Scrub the steel piston parts with a stiff brush and solvent such as CLP
Clear the carbon out of the piston grooves
Light coat of lithium grease on the piston body

cleaning.name: MOUNT AREA & THREADS
tasks: Mount area free of carbon and other debris
Remove the host's thread protector and confirm the barrel's thread pitch matches the mount before refitting

cleaning.name: BODY & FINISH
tasks: Anodized aluminum body and baffles — only chemicals safe on anodized aluminum
⚠ After shooting wet, dry every component before storage

reassembly: Put a small amount of lubricant on each baffle O-ring — Lone Wolf says it aids assembly and disassembly.

Thread the baffles back together. They are all the same and can go in any order; the can comes with eight for maximum suppression, and you may run fewer if you choose. Do not cross-thread them, or damage will occur.

Lubricate the piston first with a light coating of lithium grease (or similar) on its body. Place the piston into the suppressor body, place the spring onto the piston, then fit the piston endcap to complete the system. For a fixed or three-lug mount, install that mount into the body instead, hand tight — never a tool.
With the host unloaded and its thread protector removed, confirm the barrel's thread pitch matches the mount, then thread the suppressor onto the barrel hand tight only. Do not over-tighten.
If you feel resistance while threading it on, stop and review the instructions. If it still resists, contact Lone Wolf Arms customer service.
fncheck: Host unloaded and the can cold: the baffle stack is threaded fully together with no cross-threaded joint, the piston, spring and endcap (or the fixed or three-lug mount) are in place, and the suppressor is threaded hand tight on the barrel. On a new host, check the suppressor's alignment to the bore before shooting, or have a qualified gunsmith do it. After installation, check periodically that the can is still tight — Lone Wolf warns thread-mounted suppressors tend to loosen at the barrel or at the mount.
